comparisons.local: As higher education continues to shift to be more progressive, providing access to more students of different backgrounds, it currently is facing an obstacle. The escalating cost of tuition is growing to be a significant concern for access to higher education. The government has prioritized increasing federal financial aid to improve accessibility. However, this intervention may paradoxically worsen the rise of the cost of college, as suggested by William Bennett's famous hypothesis. As the higher education landscape evolves, a nuanced examination of tuition rise drivers is essential. This study utilizes cross-sectional data from the National Center for Education Statistics to evaluate Bennett's hypothesis, focusing on the impact of government financial aid and institutional aid on costs at public and private nonprofit colleges in the US. The study is structured around an institution’s charging variance and determinants of financial aid. The analysis reveals evidence supporting Bennett’s Hypothesis, indicating a correlation between financial aid and tuition costs across various institutions.

comparisons.local: In the past few years, tax credits have become the fundamental policy instrument to incentivize the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) in the United States. However, contemporary research primarily focuses on new EVs, while the impact of tax credits on the used EV market remains obscure. This research aims to enhance the knowledge of EV adoption by examining the potential effects of the Used Clean Vehicle Credit, a federal program providing up to $4,000 credit to eligible consumers. We have collected sales data of used cars from 245 CarMax locations in the U.S. between 2021 and 2023 to assess the change in prices of EVs before and after implementing the tax credit. The results suggest eligible EV prices increased by $1,521, about 4.74%, once the policy was implemented. Relative to pre-owned non-EVs, EV prices have increased by $2,214, indicating that car dealers have captured a more significant portion of the subsidy amount. We also observe a continually growing trend in EV sale quantities.

comparisons.local: This study dives into the financial and sport factors that impact team market value and revenue. This study's results confirm that star players significantly enhance team value, with NBA Superstars adding nearly $500 million annually. This study discovered the prominence of a Principal-Agent Problem between star players and NBA front offices over the issue of championship pursuit. The analysis also identifies an optimal style of play for revenue generation, but that could oppose longer-term team value. These findings have critical implications for NBA front offices, owners, and coaching staffs.

comparisons.local: This paper uses Rosen's paper on hedonic pricing as a framework to analyze the determinants of used car prices found in Craigslist. Using cleaned data, we observe over 43,000 listings from 2005 to 2020 and investigate factors that affect used car prices and how they interact in this market. Results show that odometer readings and condition are the strongest factors that determine price, while manufacturers, paint color, drive type, fuel type, size, and year have more ambiguous effects that depend on certain perceived attributes or conditions.

comparisons.local: This paper intends to examine the determinants of diamond pricing using a hedonic regression framework. Using the diamonds dataset from Wickham (2016), we analyze the four C’s, also known as carat weight, cut, color, and clarity. We also wanted to go deeper into this topic and look into the depth and table to see how it impacts diamond pricing. Results have displayed that carat weight greatly influences a diamond’s price, while characteristics such as clarity, color, and cut exert positive effects. Estimates were found to be statistically significant. Our findings confirm and reassure the idea that hedonic pricing accurately captures consumer valuation of diamond attributes and support research on how diamonds are priced in the market.

records.title: Do Rural Areas Gender-Discriminate Wages More than Metropolitan Areas?
records.frontend_citation: Gonzalez, A., Montano, M., Sacks, B., Williams, J. (2026). Do Rural Areas Gender-Discriminate Wages More than Metropolitan Areas? UNLV Undergraduate Economics Working Paper Series, 3(1), 1–14 (UNLV-Econ-WPS-2026-006). https://doi.org/10.34917/40601195

comparisons.local: Do Rural Areas Gender-Discriminate Wages More than Metropolitan Areas?
comparisons.remote: Do Rural Areas Gender-Discriminate Wages More than Metropolitan Areas?

comparisons.local: This study analyzes the gender wage gap in metropolitan versus rural areas using U.S. hourly wage data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), for the period 2010-2025. The analysis uses regressions on a semi-log wage model and Blinder-Oaxaca decompositions to compare the gaps and separate the effects attributable to explained (endowment) differences from those attributable to unexplained (coefficient) differences. The semi-log wage model reveals a percentage wage decrease for females of approximately 17.4% in rural areas and 9.9% in metropolitan areas. The Blinder-Oaxaca decompositions further indicate that the unexplained (coefficient) component of the gap is substantially larger in rural areas than in metropolitan areas, while the explained (endowment) component is similar across the two areas. In conclusion, the gender wage gap persists in both rural and metropolitan areas and is more pronounced in rural areas—a pattern consistent with, though not direct proof of, greater wage discrimination in rural labor markets.

comparisons.local: This paper examines how socioeconomic and demographic factors influence low educational attainment across U.S. cities. The analysis estimates both a linear regression model and a semi-log model to evaluate how poverty, unemployment, family structure, age composition, overcrowding, racial and ethnic minority share, broadband access, and housing cost burden affect the percentage of adults without a high school diploma. The results show that poverty, overcrowding, and minority share are the strongest predictors of low educational attainment, each exhibiting positive and highly significant effects. Overall, the findings highlight the role of social factors in shaping educational outcomes in high school.

comparisons.remote: Labor Market Responses to AI: Measuring Wage Effects Across U.S. Occupations

comparisons.local: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing economies around the world, with some experts predicting an impact greater than the Industrial Revolution. As AI becomes more common in daily life and business, questions have grown about how it might affect jobs, wages, and inequality. The rise of automation and highly capable AI models has made people wonder which occupations will benefit and which might be at risk. This study looks at how exposure to AI technologies affects wage trajectories in the United States. Using occupational-level data from O*NET and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, we build an AI exposure index based on how easily tasks can be automated. We then use a fixed-effects regression model to see how AI exposure relates to changes in median wages and differences in earnings across occupations over time. Our goal is to better understand how AI influences income distribution and provide insight that could help guide policies for fairer labor market transitions as technology continues to evolve.

comparisons.local: The Effects of Neighborhood and Interior Characteristics on Residential Sale Prices
comparisons.remote: The Effects of Neighborhood and Interior Characteristics on Residential Sale Prices

comparisons.local: This study analyses to what extent certain neighborhood and interior characteristics affect residential sale prices, after accounting for standard property variables. This is important to examine in order to understand the function of the housing market, the sources of price differences, and whether residential values can be controlled by prioritizing specific desirable property features. The study is based on a dataset of approximately 330,000 observations from the Multiple Listing Service (MLS), as well as walkability data obtained from Walk Score. The data is analyzed in Stata, using three regression models with different combinations of explanatory variables. The results show that the model containing neighborhood variables has a higher explanatory power than the model with the interior variables, though the magnitude of the interior attributes’ coefficients is stronger than those of the neighborhood features. The full model, containing all variables of interest, has the highest explanatory power, suggesting that this model explains more of the price variation than the other two models, and it provides the most comprehensive specification of the variation in residential sale prices, since it does not omit any potentially important variables included in the study. Overall, this suggests that, after controlling for standard property variables, both neighborhood and interior attributes are valuable determinants of the variation in sale prices in the housing market. Moreover, further research is intended, to gain more knowledge and skills in the area, and to expand the scope of the project to hopefully get more comprehensive and accurate results.

records.frontend_citation: Keithley, J. A., Hampton, C. (2026). MLB Speed Premium. UNLV Undergraduate Economics Working Paper Series, 3(2), 1–10 (UNLV-Econ-WPS-2026-010). https://doi.org/10.34917/40601199
records.repository_citation: Keithley, J. A., Hampton, C. (2026). MLB Speed Premium. UNLV Undergraduate Economics Working Paper Series, 3 (2), 1-10. Available at: http://dx.doi.org/10.34917/40601199

comparisons.local: This study analyzes if the 2023 rule changes affected the valuation for speed in the MLB labor market. By using a log-linear wage model and including an interaction term for stolen bases and the post-2023 indicator, we test to see if there is a speed premium in salaries. After accounting for yearly effects, the results present a statistically significant increase in the marginal value of stolen bases after the rule change shock. A placebo test was used with home runs to confirm the effects were specific to speed related metrics. The results suggest that the MLB market has and is adjusting to the new speed incentives created by the rule changes.

comparisons.remote: Simple Determinants of Commercial Bank Failures

comparisons.local: This study investigates the internal and macroeconomic determinants of commercial banking failures in the United States spanning 1959 to 2025. Using a logit model and a four-quarter lag, two models are estimated: a comprehensive model (1985–2025) and an extended panel model (1960–2025). Empirical results reveal internal CAMELS metrics are primary determinants of survival; profitability and capital adequacy defends against failures, while asset quality deterioration and management inefficiencies accelerates failure. The “too big to fail” paradigm is empirically validated. Contractionary monetary policy and labor market stress increase failure probabilities. Real GDP growth exhibits a role shift predicting commercial bank failures.

comparisons.remote: Gambling Behaviors: How Do Gambling Losses Affect Future Wagers?

comparisons.local: This study looks at how previous gambling losses affect future betting behavior in online cryptocurrency gambling markets. Using roughly 50,000 real betting observations from Bustabit, the paper tests whether gamblers become more aggressive after losses or instead pull back and bet more cautiously. Using both OLS and Fixed Effects regression models, the results show that players generally reduce their wager sizes following losses rather than engage in strong loss-chasing behavior. After controlling for individual player tendencies, the Fixed Effects models show statistically significant decreases in future bet sizes after losses, suggesting that caution and loss aversion may play a larger role in online gambling behavior than traditionally assumed.

comparisons.remote: Las Vegas Casino Revenue in an Expanding Gambling Market

comparisons.local: This study examines whether expanding gambling substitutes disrupt the Las Vegas gambling industry using quarterly data from 2014 through 2025. Las Vegas casino revenue is used as the benchmark to gauge the health of Las Vegas, adjusted to Quarter 1 2014 dollars and using an OLS regression model. The results imply that online sports betting is a poor substitute for Las Vegas revenue, while online gambling shows a positive and statistically significant relationship with revenue. The findings indicate that Las Vegas is resilient despite the introduction of more competition and gambling alternatives within an industry it has traditionally known to dominate.

comparisons.local: Determinants of March Madness Tournament Advancement
comparisons.remote: Determinants of March Madness Tournament Advancement

comparisons.local: This paper examines whether tournament seed and team efficiency ratings help explain how far teams advance in the NCAA men's basketball tournament. Using Bart Torvik NCAA basketball ratings data from 2008 to 2025, I construct a team-year dataset with tournament advancement measured from 1 to 7, where higher values represent deeper runs. The main independent variables are seed, net efficiency, offensive efficiency, and defensive efficiency. Descriptive statistics, correlations, scatterplots, and OLS regressions are used to test whether better-seeded and more efficient teams advance further. The results show that seed is the strongest and most consistent predictor of advancement, but efficiency ratings still matter after controlling for seed. Net efficiency is positive and statistically significant, while offensive efficiency is positive and defensive efficiency is negative when the two sides of the ball are separated. Overall, the findings suggest that March Madness contains a large amount of randomness, but tournament success is still strongly related to team quality.
